title: Instructions decay, hooks don't
tldr: Seventeen open Claude Code sessions and no way to tell which ones were waiting on me. The fix was three lines at the end of every response — and what made it stick wasn't the instruction, it was a one-line hook that re-states it every turn.
metaDescription: Why a CLAUDE.md instruction alone stops working in long agent sessions, and how a one-line UserPromptSubmit hook fixes it — the design behind an always-on Task/Status/Next footer, open source and installable.

title: I let Claude read the proposals so I didn't have to — with a human veto
tldr: 53 Upwork proposals, all 53 with at least one red flag, and roughly 30 that never answered the screening questions. The agent I built to do the reading — open source, and structurally unable to contact a candidate.
metaDescription: An open-source TypeScript pipeline that ingests Upwork proposals, scores them with Claude against a weighted rubric, and emails a ranked shortlist — with tiers computed in code and a hard human gate before anyone is contacted.

title: Standup ends when the tickets are on the board
tldr: I turned our daily standup into a pipeline: transcript in, Slack to-dos + reconciled sprint board + filed notes out — with two human review gates and 5-10 minutes of my time instead of 1-3 hours.
metaDescription: How a single Claude Code skill turns a recorded standup into Slack to-dos, deduped sprint-board tickets, and a filed transcript — with human review gates at every irreversible step.

title: Employee ownership at acquisition: finding the structure that works
tldr: More capital for the searcher, ownership for the employees, legacy for the seller — the deal logic of employee ownership at acquisition, and the airtight sub-20% Employee Ownership Trust structure I'm building to bring to SBA lenders.
metaDescription: Employee ownership at the moment of small-business acquisition: why the deal logic works for searchers, employees, and sellers, why SBA underwriting makes it hard, and the sub-20% Employee Ownership Trust structure designed to fit a 7(a) loan cleanly.

title: I built an agent that publishes my week
tldr: The agentic pipeline behind this site's weekly essays: deterministic evidence collectors, an interview that keeps me the author, a redaction layer that earned its keep, and approval gates before anything irreversible. Open source as a Claude Code skill you can install and run on your own week.
metaDescription: How I built the agent that publishes my weekly essays: grounding rules that forbid invented accomplishments, interview-driven synthesis, credential redaction, and human approval gates — open source as an installable Claude Code skill.

title: Seven months of searching for a small business — and the calculator it produced
tldr: 78 listings inquired, 28 NDAs, three deals deep, zero closed — and the screening filter, three-approach valuation method, and open-source SBA deal calculator the search produced.
metaDescription: How seven months of small-business acquisition searching (78 inquiries, 28 NDAs, three deals taken deep) produced a screening filter, a three-approach valuation methodology, and a free open-source SBA deal calculator.

title: Oil, god, and open weights
tldr: Where I land on the week's open-weights fight — Nvidia's letter, Anthropic's answer, Packy's metaphor — after a career on the open-source side of the argument. Plus 30 commits of reliability work, a deal I walked away from, and the pipeline that drafts these posts.
metaDescription: Reflections on the open-weights debate (the Nvidia coalition letter, Anthropic's position, and 'AI is Oil, Not God'), plus what I shipped and what I'm thinking about, week of July 21–28, 2026.

title: Building for strangers
tldr: Two weeks spent dragging two projects across the line from tool to product — editable stages, spend caps, a real name and a domain — and the question underneath it: if a life is a piece of art, is this hour a good brushstroke?
metaDescription: A tool you run yourself can be sharp and unfinished at the same time. None of that survives contact with a second person. Two weeks of crossing the line from tool to product.
